title: Ticket Booking System: Complete Architecture
description: Design a scalable ticket booking system with monolith and microservice architectures using React, ASP.NET Core, Azure, and AWS.

data.text: Design a high-scale ticket booking system that supports events like concerts, sports, and theatre shows. The system must handle seat selection, hold seat reservations, process payments, issue e-tickets, and support event search — all while preventing overselling during high-demand flash sales with millions of concurrent users.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Users can search events by name, city, date, venue, and category
Users can view a real-time seat map with available/occupied/held indicators
Users can temporarily hold seats for a configurable timeout window (e.g. 10 minutes)
Users can complete booking with payment and receive a confirmation and e-ticket
Users can cancel bookings within the allowed refund window and get seats released
Organizers can create and manage events with pricing tiers (VIP, Premium, Regular)
Waitlist auto-promotion when held seats expire and are released
Booking history and downloadable e-ticket (PDF)

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Sub-100ms response time for seat map queries during a sale
Sub-500ms end-to-end booking confirmation under 10x peak load
Exactly-once booking semantics: no double-booking of any seat
Strong consistency on seat inventory — no phantom reads of sold seats
System survives a 100x traffic spike (e.g., Taylor Swift flash sale) without data loss
Horizontal scalability of booking, search, and payment components independently
Idempotent payment processing — duplicate payment requests must not charge twice
99.99% uptime for the booking path; search and admin can tolerate brief degradation

data.text: Start with a monolithic ASP.NET Core application where all bounded contexts — event catalog, seat inventory, booking, payment, and notifications — run in a single process. Use a single SQL Server database with well-defined schemas per bounded context. A background hosted service handles seat hold expiration. This validates the core seat-locking and booking-flow logic before splitting.

terms.term: - Minimal API controllers per bounded context
- Entity Framework Core with SQL Server
- Redis (StackExchange.Redis) for seat-hold cache with TTL
- Background IHostedService for seat hold expiration sweeper
- SignalR for live seat-map updates to connected clients
- Stripe SDK for payment processing with idempotency keys
- Built-in DI, logging, and health checks
- Azure App Service or AWS ECS single-service deployment
- Azure SQL or AWS RDS SQL Server
- Azure Cache for Redis or ElastiCache for seat holds
- Azure Blob Storage / S3 for e-ticket PDF generation (via PuppeteerSharp)

data.text: Split the monolith into six independently scalable microservices. Seat inventory is the hardest part — the Inventory Service uses Redis compare-and-swap (CAS) and SQL row-level locking to guarantee no overselling. The Booking Service runs a distributed Saga (Orchestration pattern via MassTransit) to coordinate hold → pay → confirm without a global transaction. Search scales independently via Azure Cognitive Search or Elasticsearch.

items: Search Service: Owns event and venue search via Azure Cognitive Search / Elasticsearch. Indexes events by name, city, date, category. Handles geo-distance queries for "events near me". Redis caches top-selling event result pages.

Inventory Service: The most critical service. Manages seat maps, holds (with Redis SET EX for TTL expiry), and inventory counters. Uses SQL row-level locking and Redis Lua CAS scripts to atomically move a seat from AVAILABLE → HELD → BOOKED. Emits SeatHeld, SeatReleased, SeatBooked events.

Booking Service: Orchestrates the booking Saga. Accepts a seat-hold token from Inventory Service, invokes Payment Service, and on success confirms the booking. Compensates (cancels hold) on payment failure or timeout. Stores booking state machine: Created → Held → Confirmed / Cancelled / Expired.

Payment Service: Processes payments via Stripe or Razorpay. Enforces idempotency using the booking ID as idempotency key. Emits PaymentSucceeded / PaymentFailed events consumed by Booking and Notification services.

Notification Service: Sends booking confirmations via email (SendGrid / SES) and SMS (Twilio / SNS). Sends seat-hold expiry warnings 2 minutes before timeout. Sends in-app push notifications via SignalR.
Review Service: Allows post-event ratings and reviews. Queries Booking Service to verify the user attended before allowing a review. Indexed by Search Service for event detail pages.

cards.title: Search / Index
cards.description: Full-text search across events, venues, and cities with geo-distance ranking
pros: Built-in AI enrichers for event categories
Handles synonyms and scoring profiles out-of-the-box

cards.title: Event Streaming
cards.description: Ingest seat-state change events at high throughput for analytics and cache invalidation

cards.title: Cache
cards.description: Seat holds with TTL expiry and Lua CAS scripts for atomic state transitions
pros: Keyspace notifications for hold expiry events
cons: Redis Cluster resharding during extreme spikes

cards.title: Database
cards.description: Strongly consistent booking and payment records with ACID guarantees
pros: Row-level locking prevents phantom seat reads
cons: Vertical scaling ceiling for write-heavy peaks

cards.title: Messaging
cards.description: Saga orchestration events, payment confirmations, and notification triggers
pros: Dead-letter queues for failed payment retries

cards.title: Object Storage
cards.description: E-ticket PDF generation and archival, venue image CDN
pros: SAS URL / pre-signed URL for secure e-ticket access
CDN integration for fast ticket download globally
cons: Eventual consistency on overwrite must be handled

data.title: When to Choose Microservices?
data.text: Start with a monolith. Split into microservices only when you have clear scaling bottlenecks, independent deployment needs, or team boundaries that justify the operational overhead.

data.title: Summary
points: Seat inventory is the hardest problem — overselling is a business-critical bug
Use Redis Lua CAS for atomic seat transitions and SQL row locking as a durable guard
The Booking Saga must be idempotent: payment idempotency key = booking ID
Search must be decoupled from booking so flash-sale traffic never breaks search
Flash sales require pre-warming caches, auto-scaling seat-hold Redis, and a CDN for event pages
SignalR live seat-map updates dramatically improve UX but require a sticky-session gateway
data.takeaway: Ticket booking systems succeed or fail on inventory accuracy under concurrency. Atomic seat locking via Redis CAS, a distributed booking Saga with exactly-once payment semantics, and a decoupled search tier are the three non-negotiable architectural decisions.
